ety.text: From Middle English risen, from Old English rīsan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīsan, from Proto-Germanic *rīsaną (“to rise”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey- (“to arise, rise”). According to Kroonen (2013), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to rise, spring”). See also raise. Cognates Cognate with Dutch rijzen (“to rise”), German reisen (“to fall”), Limburgish rieze (“to rise”), Faroese and Icelandic rísa (“to rise”), Norwegian Nynorsk risa, rise (“to rise”), Gothic *𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐌽 (*reisan, “to rise”) (whence 𐌿𐍂𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐌽 (urreisan, “to arise”)).

senses.d: To move upwards.
ex: We watched the balloon rise.
Disturbed by my footsteps, the birds rose above the treetops.

senses.d: To grow upward; to attain a certain height.
ex: This elm tree rises to a height of seventy feet.

senses.d: To slope upward.
ex: The path rises as you approach the foot of the hill.

senses.d: To appear to move upwards from behind the horizon of a planet as a result of the planet's rotation.
ex: The sun was rising in the East.

senses.d: To become erect; to assume an upright position.
ex: to rise from a chair or from a fall

senses.d: To leave one's bed; to get up.
ex:
Yellow is the colour of my true love's hair,
In the morning, when we rise

senses.d: To be resurrected.
ex: he rose from the grave;   he is risen!

senses.d: To terminate an official sitting; to adjourn.
ex: The committee rose after agreeing to the report.
It was near nine[…]before the House rose.

senses.d: To attain a higher status.
ex: Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall.
among the rising theologians of Germany

senses.d: Of a quantity, price, etc., to increase.
The process of or an action or instance of moving upwards or becoming greater.
ex: The rise of the tide.
There was a rise of nearly two degrees since yesterday.

senses.d: The process of or an action or instance of coming to prominence.
ex: The rise of the working class.
The rise of the printing press.

senses.d: An increase in a quantity, price, etc.
The amount of material extending from waist to crotch in a pair of trousers or shorts.
ex: The rise of his pants was so low that his tailbone was exposed.

senses.d: The front of a diaper.
A small hill; used chiefly in place names.
An area of terrain that tends upward away from the viewer, such that it conceals the region behind it; a slope.
ex: I went along up the bank with one eye out for pap and t'other one out for what the rise might fetch along.

senses.d: A very noticeable visible or audible reaction of a person or group.
ex: Making fun of their football team is one sure way to get a rise from a crowd.
She really got a rise from the audience when she donned a wig and talked like the president.

senses.d: The height of an arch or a step.
ex: As the rise, i.e. height, of the arch decreases, the outward thrust increases.
Each step had a rise of 170 mm and a going of 250 mm.

senses.d: The probability of a negative outcome to a decision or event.
ex: There is risk of being brutalized, arrested, imprisoned and tortured, all because I want you to know the truth about this matter.
2006, Trever Ramsey on BBC News website, Exercise 'cuts skin cancer risk' read at http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/health/4764535.stm on 14 May 2006

senses.d: The magnitude of possible loss consequent to a decision or event.
ex: Will they find the prospect of greater risk a cause for concern, rather than a gift from the right?

senses.d: The potential negative effect of an event, determined by multiplying the likelihood of the event occurring with its magnitude should it occur.
A possible adverse event or outcome.
ex: the imminent and constant risk of assassination, a risk which has shaken very strong nerves

senses.d: A type of adverse event covered under an insurance policy.
A thing (from the perspective of how likely or unlikely it is to cause an adverse effect).

senses.d: A borrower (such as a mortgage-holder or person with a credit card).
ex: A good credit rating indicates the customer is a desirable risk.

senses.d: A financial product (typically an investment).
ex: Subprime mortgages are poor risks; especially for a pension scheme.

senses.d: An entity insured by an insurer.
To incur risk of (an unwanted or negative outcome).
ex: These people are putting themselves in danger by physically being on or near to the railway lines and risking serious injury.

senses.d: To incur risk of harming or jeopardizing.
ex: England captain David Beckham has warned Wayne Rooney not to risk his long-term future by rushing his return from injury.

senses.d: To incur risk as a result of (doing something).
ex: After coming to New York, I decided to risk cycling again.
